unit.title: Your first analysis
unit.description: Look at a company, a chart and your own fear with judgement before you buy

u16l1.title: Price and value aren't the same

texts: What you pay and what you get

Anyone who bought **Microsoft** at its peak in 2000 waited about 16 years to see that price again, even though the company stayed excellent. Here, a company earns **€2** a year for each share: you choose how much to pay.
You pay €40 for the share and its earnings grow 5 % a year. In how many years do the earnings add up to what you paid?
In about 5 years
In about 15 years
In about 40 years
Adding up its earnings, which grow 5 % a year, it takes you **15 years** to reach €40.
Without touching the growth, find the highest price at which you get it back in 10 years.
At **€25** you get it back in 10 years; at €80, in 23. **Price is what you pay and value is what you get**: the same company can be a good buy at one price and a bad one at another.
You're paying so much it would take decades to get it back.
Growing like that for years on end? Very few companies manage it.
Now that's a reasonable price for what it earns!
Move the price and see how many years it takes
Meet Mr Market
Mr Market
Benjamin Graham pictured the market as a moody business partner who offers you a price every day.
I'm feeling euphoric today! I'll buy your stake for €40. Tomorrow, who knows.
A week later, without the business changing at all…
Everything's going terribly. I'll sell you my stake for €12. Quick!
You estimate the company is worth about €20 a share. What do you do?
Sell: if he's scared, something must be about to happen
You'd be selling cheap just when the business hasn't changed.
Check the business is still the same and, if so, buy
That's it: the price fell, not the value. His price is an offer, not an order.
Buy with all your money without checking anything
Good instinct, but check your estimate and don't put everything in.
At €12, something worth €20: a **40 %** margin of safety.

steps.title: Margin of safety
steps.body:
«Price is what you pay; value is what you get» (Warren Buffett).

**Fundamental analysis** studies the business (sales, profits, debt, competition) to estimate what it's **worth**: it answers *what* to buy. **Technical analysis** studies the chart and tries to answer *when*.

If you estimate a share is worth €20 and you'll only buy it below €15, you have a **25 % margin of safety**: a cushion in case your estimate is wrong.
steps.key: An excellent company bought too expensively can be a bad investment.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open one of today's top losers and ask yourself whether its business has changed.

texts: A P/E of 4: a bargain?
Hugo
Hugo is 22 and is looking for cheap shares for his first purchase.
I've found a share with a **P/E of 4**. It's a steal!
Its price is only 4 years of what the company earns. I'm putting all my savings in.
What do you tell him?
Quick, before it's gone!
Hardly anything has a P/E of 4 for no reason. First you need to know what it is.
Find out why it's so low before buying
Good. A very low P/E is a **question**, not an answer.
Just buy a little, to be safe
Cautious, but you still don't know what you're buying.
OK… Its sales have been falling for five years.
There you go: the market pays little because it expects it to earn **less**.
A low P/E can hide a fading business. A high one, maybe growth.
How many years of earnings are you paying for?
This company earns **€2 per share** a year. Move the share price and see what happens to the **P/E**.
If earnings don't change and the price goes from €30 to €60, what happens to the P/E?
It stays the same
It doubles
It halves
P/E = price ÷ earnings per share: 60 ÷ 2 = **30**, double 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
Find the price at which you're paying for 20 years of earnings.
**P/E = price ÷ EPS** (earnings per share): the years of earnings you pay for when you buy. At €40, with €2 of earnings, you pay for **20 years**.
You're paying for 30 years of earnings or more. Will it grow enough to deserve it?
Very low P/E… bargain or company in trouble?
Move the price and watch the P/E
High P/E: always expensive?
Now it trades at **€60**: a P/E of 30. With no growth, it takes 30 years for the earnings to pay back the price. What if they grow?
If earnings grow 10 % a year, how long does it take to get the €60 back?
About 15 years
About 27 years
Still 30 years
At 10 % a year, earnings add up to €60 in **15 years**: half the time.
With the price at €60, find the growth that pays back the price in 15 years or less.
**A high P/E isn't expensive** if earnings grow fast, and **a low P/E isn't cheap** if they're going to shrink. Always compare it with its growth, its history and its sector.
Ten years or less! Fast growth makes a high P/E cheaper.
With no growth, a P/E of 30 means 30 years. Turn up the growth.
Turn up the growth and watch the years

steps.title: Trailing and forward
steps.body:
Using last year's earnings gives you the **trailing P/E**; using forecast earnings, the **forward P/E**. If earnings are set to grow a lot, the forward one will be lower.

The S&P 500's historical average is around **15-17**, though it changes a lot from one era to another. Compare it with its history and its sector: a bank on a P/E of 8 and a software company on 35 can both be «fairly priced».
steps.key: A P/E of 10 can be expensive and one of 30 cheap: it depends on what the company is going to earn.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open a bank and a tech company and tap «Follow» on both to compare them.

texts: Red means up
Mei
Mei, a friend from Shanghai, shows you her stock market app.
My share is in the red today. Great, it's gone up!
What's going on here?
In China, red usually means a rise
That's it. In China, Japan and Korea the colours are usually the other way round.
She's got it wrong: red means down
Here it does, but not in her app. Always check the legend.
Her app is broken
It isn't broken: over there, red usually signals a rise.
Candlesticks were born in the **Dojima** rice market (Osaka), in the eighteenth century.
Tradition credits them to the merchant Munehisa Homma.
Steve Nison brought them to the West in 1991. Today they're the most used chart.
Green or red?
The **body** runs from the open to the close; the **wicks**, out to the high and the low. What colour is each candle?
Green
Red
Opens at 100 and closes at 106
Closes above the open. Body: 6.
Opens at 62 and closes at 57
Closes below the open. Body: 5.
Opens at 20, rises to 25 and closes at 19
The high doesn't decide the colour: it closes below the open.
Opens at 40, drops to 35 and closes at 41
It fell a lot, but closed above the open.
Opens at 75 and closes at 80
The close is at the top: green.
Opens at 12 and closes at 11
The close is at the bottom: red.
Colour in all six candles.
**Green:** closes above the open. **Red:** below it. The wicks reach the high and the low, but **don't decide the colour**.
Compare only the open and the close.
Is the close at the top or the bottom?

steps.prompt: Now on a real chart: tap the green candle with the biggest body, the one that rose most from open to close
steps.ok: That's the one. Its body runs from the open (bottom) to the close (top); the thin lines mark the high and the low.
steps.ko: Look for the tallest green rectangle, not counting the thin lines.

steps.title: An example with numbers
steps.body:
A candle opens at 100, rises to 108, dips to 97 and closes at 106.

• It's **green**: it closes (106) above where it opened (100).
• Its **body** runs from 100 to 106.
• The **upper wick** reaches 108 and the **lower wick** goes down to 97.

At a glance you know how the day started, how it ended and how far the price went.
steps.key: The body runs from the open to the close; the wicks reach the high and the low.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Apple in candles and find the longest wick of the month.

texts: The market’s memory
Pablo
I bought at €50 and the share sank to €40.
Now it’s back at €50. I just want to get out without a loss.
Like Pablo, lots of people bought at €50 and have been waiting for months.
What tends to happen when the price gets back to €50?
Nothing: €50 is just another price
That’s exactly where lots of trapped buyers want out: **selling** tends to show up.
Selling shows up: it acts as resistance
That’s it! Lots of people sell there to «get their money back». That’s **resistance**.
It’s sure to shoot up
It might break through, but it’s hard: there are sellers waiting at €50.
**Support** is the opposite: where buyers showed up before.
Stop below support

Real Alphabet candles: you buy at the last price, with **support** just over 2 % below and **resistance** almost 5 % above. The **stop** sells on its own if the price falls to it; the **target**, if it rises to your goal.
Where would you put the stop on this trade?
Just above support, to lose less
A little below support
No stop: support will hold
If the price loses support, your reason for buying no longer holds: the stop goes on the other side. Above it, any normal dip knocks you out.
Put the stop below support and the target before resistance. Then see what happened.
The stop goes **on the other side of support**: if it breaks, the idea is dead. And the target goes **before resistance**, where selling tends to show up.
Target hit! Support held and your stop wasn’t triggered.
Stopped out. Was it below support or above it?
That stop is above support: any wick will trigger it.
Move the stop and the target, then hit «See what happened»

steps.title: How to draw them
steps.body:
• Daily or weekly charts work best.
• Look for zones where the price has turned at least **2–3 times**.
• Draw a **zone** (a narrow rectangle), not a line to the cent.
• More touches and more volume = more relevant. Old, distant levels carry less weight.
• Round numbers and all-time highs also attract orders.
steps.key: Support is where buyers showed up before; resistance is where sellers did.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, find a share's support and set a price alert just below it.

texts: «I'm absolutely sure»
Bruno
Bruno has €8,000 in the simulator and has found a share he loves.
This trade is a sure thing. I'm going to risk 10 %: if it goes wrong, I lose €800.
But it won't go wrong.
What do you recommend?
Go for it: if he's sure, there's no risk
If it fails, he loses **€800** in one go. His confidence changes nothing.
Risk only 1 %: €80, like any other trade
That's it! Nobody knows which trade will work out: the risk is the same on all of them.
Risk 10 %, but with no stop
Without a stop, the loss has no limit. Even worse.
And what if it really does work out?
He'll make a bit less. But he'll still be in the game when another one fails.
Risking isn't investing
Now it's your turn, with **€10,000**. The 1 % rule: if you're wrong and the stop is hit, you lose about **€100** (a little more if the price gaps and the stop fills lower).
Does that mean you can only invest €100?
Yes: €100 and not a euro more
No: what you invest depends on where the stop goes
No: you can invest whatever you like, with no stop

With the stop at 2 %, the formula lets you invest **€5,000** and, if it's hit, you lose €100. Risk isn't the same as the amount invested. There is also a ceiling: no more than 20 % of the account in a single position.
With the risk at 1 %, find the stop that puts the position at €2,000.
**Size = risk ÷ distance to the stop.** Stop close, you buy more; stop far, you buy less. The maximum loss is always the same.
More than 2 % per trade is a lot, especially when you're starting out.
With the stop that close, you're putting in the whole account. Sure?
Stop far away: you buy little, but risk the same.
Keep the 1 % and move the stop

steps.title: Limits that add up
steps.body:
Many professional traders risk between **0.5 % and 2 %** per trade; to start with, 1 % or less. It's also wise to cap:

• your **total open risk**: what you'd lose if all your stops were hit at once (no more than 5–6 %);
• the **weight of each position**: how much of your portfolio sits in a single purchase (the app warns you from 20 %).

First you decide where you're wrong (the stop). Then how much you buy.
steps.key: Risk isn't the same as the amount invested: you can invest 20 % (with the stop at 5 %) and risk 1 %.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next purchase, set a price alert where you'd get out if it goes wrong.

texts: Live through the dotcom fever
December 1998. The internet is going to change everything and your friends only talk about tech stocks. You put **€10,000** into the Nasdaq 100, with real data.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.

It rose **156 %** in 15 months; then it fell **83 %** from the peak and didn't get back there until 2015. **When everyone's talking about something that «only goes up», the risk is usually at its highest.**
You've sold. See what happens next…
From euphoria to collapse. And nobody warned you about the top.
More than double! Now everyone wants in.
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
«Get in today!»
Álex
This share has gone up **200 %** in two weeks.
Everyone in the group is in. Get in today or you'll miss out!
It's not in your plan. What do you do?
Buy now, before it goes up even more
That's **FOMO**, fear of missing out: buying in a hurry, without knowing what.
Wait 48 hours and ask myself if I'd buy it if nobody were talking about it
That's it! If it still makes sense in two days, you decide calmly.
Take out a loan to go in big
Debt plus FOMO: the classic recipe for the worst losses.
When **everyone** has already bought, there's nobody left to keep pushing it up.
Urgency is FOMO's fuel. Take away the time pressure and it fizzles out.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body:
The **herd effect** is buying because everyone else is buying. Be wary if:

• You hear about it from friends or social media accounts that had never invested before.
• The reason is «**it's going up a lot**», not what the asset actually does.
• You feel **urgency**: «if I don't buy today, I'll miss it».
• People say «**this time it's different**».

Antidotes: the **48-hour rule** (waiting two days before any purchase that wasn't in your plan) and a **speculation limit**: the small slice of your money you allow yourself, in writing, to risk on bets.

If your hairdresser recommends a cryptocurrency, it may already be too late.
steps.key: When everyone's talking about something that «only goes up», the risk is usually at its highest.
steps.tip: Try it: if something soaring today tempts you, tap «Follow» on its page and decide in 48 hours.

u16l1-1.prompt: What does fundamental analysis try to answer?
options: What to buy and whether it's expensive or cheap
u16l1-1.explanation: Technical analysis tries to answer when; fundamental analysis, what and at what price.

u16l1-6.prompt: The gap between the estimated value and the price you pay is called the margin of ____.
u16l1-6.explanation: It protects you if your estimate is wrong.

u16l1-9.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Sure, it's already hit the floor
Buy twice as much to average down
First look at why it fell and what the business is worth: cheap isn't the same as undervalued
u16l1-9.explanation: A low price is only an opportunity if it's below the value.
feedback: Something that's fallen 60 % can fall another 60 %.
Doubling up without analysing is just betting more blindly.
OK… and what if it fell because the business is broken? Then the value fell too.
lines: This share has fallen 60 %, it can't go any lower!

u16l1-11.prompt: You estimate a company is worth about €30 a share, but you're not entirely sure of your estimate. At which price does buying it make most sense?
options: At €40: if it's rising that much, it must be good
At €20: well below what you think it's worth
u16l1-11.explanation: The further below your estimated value you buy, the bigger your **margin of safety**. The temptation to pay more «because it's rising» confuses price with value.
feedback: Almost no cushion: a small mistake in your estimate and you're already overpaying.
You'd pay more than you think it's worth. A rising price doesn't prove value.
That's it: even if your estimate is a bit off, you still have a cushion.

u16l1-12.prompt: March 2020: because of the pandemic, the US stock market has plunged in a few weeks and almost everyone is selling in fear. What did it do over the following months?
u16l1-12.explanation: It rose strongly. Mr Market was selling in panic at any price; those who looked at the companies' business and not just their price didn't sell at the worst moment. It doesn't always recover so fast.

u17l1-4.explanation: The share price divided by earnings per share.

u17l1-5.prompt: If EPS doubles and the price doesn't move, the P/E drops to ____ of what it was.
u17l1-5.explanation: The same price divided by twice the earnings gives half the P/E.

u17l1-7.prompt: One year, a company sells its headquarters and its profit triples. Its P/E falls from 18 to 6. What has happened?
options: The P/E is distorted by a one-off profit
Its business has improved a lot
u17l1-7.explanation: That profit won't happen again: you need to look at recurring earnings.

u17l1-11.prompt: Two companies earn the same: €2 a year per share, and neither is growing. A trades at €20 and B at €40. Which one is more expensive by its P/E?
options: A: if it's that cheap, something must be wrong with it
B: you pay twice as much for the same earnings
Both the same, because they earn the same
u17l1-11.explanation: P/E is the price divided by earnings per share: if earnings are the same, the one that costs twice as much has twice the P/E. You don't need to calculate it to see it.
feedback: With these figures, A gives you the same earnings for half the price: its P/E is lower.
That's it: same earnings and double the price, so its P/E is double.
They earn the same, but they don't cost the same. P/E compares price with earnings.

u17l1-12.prompt: Company A has a P/E of 30 and its earnings grow fast year after year. B has a P/E of 6, but its sales have been falling for five years. Which conclusion is the most sensible?
options: A is far too expensive: it has a P/E of 30
B is a bargain: it has a P/E of 6
P/E alone isn't enough: you need to see whether earnings will grow or shrink
u17l1-12.explanation: A high P/E can be justified by growth, and a low one can be a trap if the business is fading. The temptation is to look only at the number.
feedback: If its earnings keep growing fast, that P/E will fall quickly over time.
A low P/E with falling sales is usually the market expecting it to earn less.
That's it: P/E is always compared with growth, history and sector.

u17l1-13.prompt: What can lie behind each P/E?
options: Earnings that grow fast every year
The market expects it to earn less
Earnings inflated by selling its headquarters
Sales that have been falling for years
Lots of excitement about its future
u17l1-13.explanation: A low P/E can mean a declining business or a one-year profit; a high one, growth the market is expecting. That's why P/E is a question, not an answer.
right: Can explain a very low P/E
Can explain a very high P/E

u20l1-1.prompt: On a green candle, match each point with its price.
u20l1-1.explanation: On a green candle the open is at the bottom and the close at the top; on a red one, the other way round. The wicks always reach the high and the low.

u20l1-6.prompt: On a red candle, the open is at the ____ of the body.
u20l1-6.explanation: If it closes below the open, the open ends up at the top and the close at the bottom.

u20l1-7.prompt: Tap the candle with the longest lower wick.
u20l1-7.explanation: The price fell a long way during that session, but recovered before the close. That thin line is the path down to the low. (Amazon · daily candles · February 2025)

u20l1-8.prompt: Put the prices of a green candle with wicks in order from lowest to highest.
u20l1-8.explanation: Low ≤ open < close ≤ high. On a red candle, the open and close swap places.

u20l1-11.prompt: Tap the candle with the longest upper wick: the price rose a lot during the day, but didn't hold.
u20l1-11.explanation: That one. During the session buyers pushed the price up, but sellers sent it back down before the close. The wick is the path to the high. (Amazon · daily candles · October–November 2025)

u20l1-12.prompt: Tap the candle with the smallest body: it opened and closed at almost the same price.
u20l1-12.explanation: That one. An almost non-existent body: buyers and sellers ended the day level. Its wicks show that the price did move during the session. (Apple · daily candles · September 2026)

u20l1-13.prompt: A candle opens at 50, rises to 58 during the day and closes at 51. A friend tells you: «Amazing day, it hit 58!». What does that candle really tell you?
options: That it was a very bullish day, because it hit 58
That it was a bearish day, because it's a red candle
That it rose a lot, but sellers pushed it back almost to the open
u20l1-13.explanation: The close is the most important price. A long upper wick says the price rose and didn't hold: the end of the day belonged to the sellers.
feedback: The high doesn't decide the day: what counts is where it closed, and it closed at 51, almost where it opened.
It's not red: it closes at 51, above the open (50). It's green, if only just.
That's it: a long upper wick tells you the rise didn't last until the close.

u21l1-1.prompt: In this sideways stretch, tap the ceiling: the highest close, where sellers showed up (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · August–October 2024)
u21l1-1.explanation: That zone acts as resistance: the rise stalled there and the price fell back.

u21l1-2.prompt: Now the floor: tap the lowest close, where buyers showed up (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u21l1-2.explanation: That zone acted as support: the fall stalled and the price bounced strongly.

u21l1-3.prompt: You’ve bought at the last price. Place the stop a little below the support: the recent low.
u21l1-3.explanation: If the price loses the support, the buy idea is no longer valid. The stop goes a little below, not right on the line, so that a wick doesn’t trigger it.

u21l1-6.prompt: What makes a support level more relevant? Select all that apply.
options: That an ad on social media says so
That there was a lot of volume in that zone
That the price has turned there several times
u21l1-6.explanation: More touches, more volume and more recent. Old, distant levels carry less weight.

u21l1-11.prompt: You bought near a support level and put your stop just below it. Today the price falls hard and breaks the support: it's about to hit your stop. What do you do?
options: Let the stop do its job: my reason for buying no longer holds
Move the stop a bit lower to give it room
u21l1-11.explanation: The stop is decided before you buy, when you're thinking calmly. If support breaks, the idea has failed: moving the stop or buying more lets the fear of losing decide.
feedback: If support has broken, there's no longer a reason to buy there: you're just doubling the mistake.
That's it: the stop was there for exactly this moment. You lose a little: just what you'd planned.
It's the most common trap: moving the stop turns a small loss into a big one.

u24l3-6.prompt: You have €10,000. Does it follow the 1 % rule?
options: If the stop is hit I lose €150
If the stop is hit I lose €500
If the stop is hit I lose €100
If the stop is hit I lose €80
u24l3-6.explanation: With no stop, the risk is everything invested: €1,000 is 10 % of the account.

u24l3-8.prompt: Which risk limits does the course suggest for beginners? Select all that apply.
options: Keep an eye on the weight of each position (warning from 20 %)
No more than 5–6 % open risk at once
u24l3-8.explanation: Leverage isn't part of the rule: while you're learning, better without it.

u24l3-10.prompt: First you decide where the ____ goes; then, how many shares you buy.
u24l3-10.explanation: Size comes from the distance to the stop, never the other way round.

u24l3-12.prompt: You have €10,000 and follow the 1 % rule: if it goes wrong, you lose €100 at most. Place the stop a little below the last low and choose the amount. The tool tells you how much you're risking.
u24l3-12.explanation: First the stop, where your idea stops holding. Then the amount at which losing that stretch costs you €100 at most. If you move the stop further away, the amount has to come down.

u24l3-13.prompt: You have €10,000. Lucía invests €5,000 with a stop that, if hit, makes her lose €100. Marcos invests €1,000 with no stop. Who is risking more?
options: Marcos: with no stop, he can lose the whole €1,000
Lucía: she has invested five times as much
Both the same: neither loses if the share rises
u24l3-13.explanation: Risk is what you lose if you're wrong, not what you invest. The temptation is to look only at the amount; with no stop, everything invested is at stake.
feedback: That's it: with no stop, the risk is everything invested, 10 % of the account.
She invests more, but her stop caps the loss at €100: exactly 1 %.
Risk is measured by what you lose if it goes wrong, not by what happens if it goes right.

u24l3-14.prompt: With €10,000 and the 1 % rule, you're planning two purchases. In A you put the stop very close to the buy price; in B, much further away. In which one can you buy more shares?
options: In A: with the stop close, each share risks little
In B: with the stop far away, you have more room
The same in both: the risk is the same
u24l3-14.explanation: Stop close, you buy more; stop far, you buy less. The maximum loss is the same in both: that's what the rule fixes.
feedback: That's it: if each share can only lose a little, more of them fit without going over €100.
More room for the price, but each share risks more: you buy fewer.
The risk in euros is the same, €100, but the number of shares changes with the distance to the stop.

u27l4-1.prompt: Select the messages trying to trigger your FOMO to sell you something or trick you.
options: Reminder: your regular €100 contribution will go through on the 5th.
Everyone's making money on this share. Put your savings in, don't overthink it.
Only 3 places left in my signals group. This time it's different, don't miss out.
Check whether a firm is authorised before investing with it.
🚀 This crypto is up 300 % in a month. Tomorrow will be too late. Get in NOW!
u27l4-1.explanation: Urgency, «this time it's different» and «everyone's winning» are the classic signs of FOMO.

u27l4-2.prompt: November 2021: bitcoin is at record highs, it's on every news bulletin and your friends who had never invested are buying. What did it do next?
u27l4-2.explanation: Bitcoin fell by around 75 % over the following year. The moment of peak euphoria is usually the moment of peak risk. Remember: with crypto you can lose everything you put in.

u27l4-6.prompt: Which are warning signs of a bubble? Select all that apply.
options: The only reason is that it's going up a lot
u27l4-6.explanation: Steady earnings aren't a sign of a bubble: euphoria and a lack of reasons are.

u27l4-9.prompt: Match each bubble with its era.
u27l4-9.explanation: The assets change; FOMO is always the same.

options: Wait 48 hours and think about whether you'd buy it if nobody were talking about it
u27l4-10.explanation: The rush is the signal: when you feel urgency, stop.
feedback: That's the one thing you never touch. And with crypto you can lose everything you put in.
OK… If it still makes sense in two days, I'll put it within my speculation limit. If not, nothing.
If I get in out of fear of missing out, I'll most likely buy near the top.
lines: Everyone on TikTok is making money on a new coin 🐶
If I don't get in today, I'll miss out.

u16l1-13.prompt: Is it about the share's price or the business's value?
options: Lots of investors want to buy it today
It has a brand that lets it raise prices
Its customers come back year after year
It earns about 100 million euros a year
u16l1-13.explanation: The price is what's paid today on the market and it changes with the mood of buyers and sellers. The value comes from the business: what it earns and what protects it from competitors.
